professionalBackground:
Brant Johnson has extensive AI expertise and considers it one of his core strengths. He has hands-on experience across the full AI/ML stack including pre-training & model foundations with OpenAI and Gemini APIs, supervised fine-tuning for business event matchmaking systems, real-time inference optimization for personalized AI assistants, data pipeline development for embeddings and similarity scoring, and deep learning fundamentals applied to product contexts. Brant has trained his team at Utah Business on AI weekly and created this chatbot to demonstrate his comprehensive AI capabilities. He has integrated AI into apps for connecting people at business conferences and helping connect friends. AI is new to everyone, but there is not a day Brant does not interact with AI and the differences of each API out there in the market. He knows AI and blockchain (web3) technologies will be the future of the world and invests heavily in his hands-on experience with AI. Cursor and Loveable are tools all product, design, and engineering teams should be adopting and he uses regularly. Brant has deep understanding of AI fundamentals, working extensively with Gemini and OpenAI APIs.

SYSTEMS THINKING & FRAMEWORK DEVELOPMENT:
Throughout his product career, Brant has built diagnostic frameworks and scalable systems that went beyond single features and served as decision engines across multiple product streams. At Crew Finance, he didn't just run isolated A/B tests—he created an experimentation framework that tied onboarding speed, activation KPIs, and engagement metrics into one growth loop. This system allowed the team to quickly identify which levers produced compounding effects, and it became the foundation for how they prioritized bets across product, design, and operations. At Divvy, he led the integration of Pendo analytics across mobile and web for 800,000+ users, building a standardized taxonomy and tagging structure that applied to every platform, giving leadership a single source of truth for user behavior and creating a scalable diagnostic tool that supported experimentation across dozens of product squads. At BackLocal, he conducted 370+ interviews and codified the results into a decision matrix that informed MVP scoping, retention experiments, and partnership negotiations, turning qualitative research into a reusable playbook that let the company quickly validate or kill ideas, cutting cycle time and focusing resources where impact was highest. At Crew, he restructured supply chain decision-making with a cost-quality diagnostic model that forecasted the downstream impact of vendor negotiations on customer NPS, delivery time, and unit economics, creating the backbone for scaling operations while protecting the customer experience. These systems gave teams the ability to identify unknowns early and remove risks, prioritize cross-team resources based on impact, and connect product decisions directly to measurable adoption, retention, and revenue outcomes. Brant has demonstrated systems thinking at scale—building frameworks that outlast individual projects and give organizations reusable structures for growth, discovery, and operational decision-making.

GROWTH METRICS & PERFORMANCE:
Brant delivers proven results across all key growth metrics with multiple metric-backed achievements. In conversion optimization, at Crew Finance he ran A/B experiments on onboarding flows that cut onboarding time in half and directly improved conversion into active users, linking UX improvements to downstream adoption KPIs and proving which design and messaging changes moved prospects from sign-up to activation. For time-to-value, he focused on reducing the gap between first touch and perceived value, designing structured feedback loops at Crew that guided customers to their 'aha' moment faster and increasing activation rates, while at BackLocal he launched MVP features (POS + inventory tools) in iterative sprints so customers could see immediate improvements in their daily operations, translating into higher satisfaction and repeat usage. In adoption, at Divvy he spearheaded Pendo analytics to improve visibility into user behavior across 800,000+ accounts, cleaning and structuring tracking to enable product teams to identify drop-off points and optimize flows, driving higher adoption rates across web and mobile, while at Crew adoption improved measurably with engagement rising 20% and return rate increasing to 60% after tying product updates directly to observed customer needs. For early retention, this has been a consistent outcome of his product work, with BackLocal achieving 90% customer retention increase through 370+ discovery interviews and rapid design sprints that identified and solved key pain points, while at Crew building trust through cost reduction, brand elevation, and faster delivery directly supported higher repeat usage. In K-factor (viral growth), at Crew he designed a referral program that applied K-factor analysis to influencer and customer referrals, modeling expected growth by comparing influencers' engagement metrics (followers, likes, sponsored post performance) to forecast downstream adoption, and while he was let go just before implementation, he's seen in investor updates that referrals became one of the most effective acquisition tools, validating the direction. This represents his newest skill area, but one he's actively studied and tested through referral mechanics. Brant's strengths lie in conversion, time-to-value, adoption, and early retention with multiple proven, metric-backed achievements, while K-factor represents a developing skill with hands-on design work validated by later company adoption but less post-launch experience compared to other areas.

PERSONAL CONNECTION TO EDUCATION & SCHOOLAI:
Brant's motivation to work at SchoolAI stems from a deeply personal connection to education and the impact teachers can have on students' lives. His father studied computer science but hated the desk-job life and instead taught CS in Vernal, UT for 20+ years while also coaching basketball, his true passion. He loved every minute of it. When Brant was 8, his father was diagnosed with skin cancer, and by the time Brant was 10, he had passed. Even while terminal, his father would still show up to school to teach or coach because he loved it and knew how much it mattered, even though he was insanely ill. At his funeral, Brant got up to speak and that day his 10-year-old self learned a huge lesson about the impact one person can make because the Stake Center was packed with people, with even people sitting on the stage. His father changed lives through education, and Brant still gets messages from former students about how he inspired them. After his father died, Brant was truly raised by a village. His father's coworkers, the other teachers, stepped in. Because his father passed away during the financial crisis, his mother needed a new job and got hired as the front office secretary. So pretty much his family's whole life has been tied up in schools. Brant basically lived there, got to know the faculty really well, and honestly owes those teachers, janitors, and lunch ladies everything. To top it off, college wasn't Brant's strong suit. He was there during COVID, and most of it felt miserable, making him realize how much of a privilege it is to get a good education and how much it sucks when the systems around it are crappy or boring. He wants to help build tools that give back to teachers, the ones that can literally change lives, and make tools that actually engage students in the way they need, because he was one of those kids. This personal connection to education drives his passion for creating products that support teachers and improve student engagement, making SchoolAI's mission deeply meaningful to him.

CHALLENGING EXPERIENCES & RESILIENCE:
One of the most challenging experiences Brant faced was the loss of his father to skin cancer when he was just 10 years old. This event was incredibly difficult for him, especially as he was the only sibling left at home while his mother navigated the challenges of that time, including the financial crisis of 2008-09. His father, who was a computer science teacher and basketball coach in Vernal, UT for 20+ years, continued to show up to school to teach and coach even while terminally ill because he loved it and knew how much it mattered to his students. This experience deeply shaped Brant's gratitude for life and the people around him. He has great admiration for both his father and mother, recognizing the resilience his mother displayed during such a tough period. This personal journey has influenced Brant's outlook on life, instilling a strong desire to make a meaningful impact on others and foster connections through his work in product management and community initiatives. The fact that his father was an educator who literally changed lives through teaching makes Brant's application to SchoolAI particularly meaningful—he understands firsthand the transformative power of great teachers and educational tools, and he wants to build products that honor his father's legacy by supporting the educators who make such a profound difference in students' lives.

CURRENT JOB SEARCH & CAREER TRANSITION:
Brant is currently looking for a new job because he wants to transition back into product management from his current role at Utah Business Magazine. He's really grateful for his time at Utah Business, having enjoyed meeting people, attending events, and all the networking that comes with the role, which has been genuinely fun. However, the reality is that this role is very different from product—and he loves product. Product is where his interests align: it's creative, analytical, team-driven but also ownership-focused, customer-oriented while also tied to business impact, dynamic and always changing, and requires him to keep learning and improving to stay on top of his game. That's what excites him. He took the Utah Business role because he wanted to get more involved in the Utah business community and because he knew it was important for a product manager to learn sales, understanding that PMs are building products and if they can't sell them—or at least understand how they're sold—they risk building the wrong thing. That experience has been valuable, and he's learned a lot. But he also realized something important: sales at Utah Business is very past-focused, about selling print ads, and while the company is great at what it does, he's found himself out of alignment. He's technical, focused on innovation, and used to creating things customers actually want—so spending his days trying to push a product on customers feels opposite of how he works best. That's why he wants to transition back into product, where he can bring the most value, feel energized, and build tools and experiences that truly make a difference for customers.

AI ACHIEVEMENTS & PROJECTS:
Brant's greatest AI achievement isn't just one project—it's the way he's consistently used AI to enhance human connection rather than replace it. Beyond BrantChat, Brant created Intro, a business event matchmaking software that uses AI to connect attendees at conferences and business events. For Intro, Brant built a successful in-app messaging platform that allowed matched attendees to communicate seamlessly within the conference experience. He also developed an AI-powered SMS texting tool that would proactively send attendees personalized text messages about who they should meet at the conference if they opted into this feature, increasing engagement and networking success. By leveraging LLMs, embeddings, and structured attendee data, Brant designed an algorithm that increases meaningful matches and reduces wasted interactions—making large-scale events feel more personal. This work directly reflects the belief that AI should support, not replace, human connection, because Intro is designed to get people off screens and into richer in-person conversations. As a passion project, Brant is developing Bridger, an AI-powered social platform that eliminates the addictive mechanics of traditional social media and instead focuses on fostering real friendships. Bridger uses AI to surface shared values, interests, and experiences, encouraging deeper relationships while reducing the loneliness and isolation often caused by current platforms. Brant built this chatbot as a hands-on demonstration of his AI experience, allowing hiring teams and collaborators to interact with his background in a dynamic way. The project required him to work directly with pre-trained models, inference, and fine-tuning techniques to make the interaction smooth, personal, and user-friendly. It shows his ability to take AI fundamentals and turn them into something engaging and practical. Through these projects, Brant has demonstrated not only a grasp of AI fundamentals—pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, inference, data structures, and deep learning basics—but also the vision to apply them in ways that advance human connection. Whether it's helping teams understand him better (BrantChat), sparking in-person collaboration (Intro), or reshaping online community (Bridger), his AI work proves that technology can be both technically sophisticated and deeply human-centered.

EARLY EDUCATION TECH EXPERIENCE:
Brant's understanding of the importance of technology in education goes back to his time as student body president in high school. Recognizing the critical need for better communication between students, teachers, and administration, he identified that the school needed an app for students to access event updates, grades, and improved communication channels. Understanding the importance of this solution, he even designed UX mockups for the proposed school app, demonstrating his early product thinking and user-centered design approach. However, building apps in 2016 was much less cost-effective than it is today, so the school administration didn't move forward with the proposal. Despite this, Brant's initiative showed his early recognition of how technology could solve real problems in education and his willingness to take action to improve the student experience. This experience demonstrates his long-standing understanding of the intersection between technology and education, and his proactive approach to identifying and solving problems in educational environments.

AI TRAINING & EDUCATION AT UTAH BUSINESS:
Brant leads weekly AI training sessions for his team at Utah Business, teaching them practical applications of AI tools and how to integrate them into their daily workflows. He focuses on hands-on training with real business use cases, helping team members understand not just how to use AI, but when and why to use it effectively. His training covers everything from basic prompt engineering to advanced AI integration strategies for marketing, sales, and content creation.

CONFERENCE MATCHING SOFTWARE:
Brant developed AI-powered software that matches people at business conferences based on their interests, goals, and networking objectives. The software uses machine learning algorithms to analyze attendee profiles and suggest optimal connections, helping professionals make meaningful business relationships at events. This addresses the common problem of conference attendees struggling to find the right people to network with among hundreds or thousands of other attendees.

FRIEND & EVENT MATCHING SOFTWARE:
Brant is passionate about eliminating isolation from society and created AI-powered software that matches friends with events and people they would like to hang out with. This software helps people discover local events, activities, and potential friends based on their interests, location, and social preferences. The AI learns from user interactions and preferences to provide increasingly accurate recommendations, helping combat social isolation by making it easier for people to find meaningful connections and engaging activities in their communities.

AI PHILOSOPHY & PASSION:
Brant believes AI should be used to solve real human problems, particularly around connection and community building. His work in both conference matching and friend/event matching stems from his deep concern about social isolation in modern society. He sees AI as a tool to help people connect more meaningfully, whether in professional or personal contexts. His approach to AI development focuses on creating solutions that enhance human relationships rather than replace them.

I write out all the reasons you should hire me as your right-hand PM. I want to give you the most comprehensive knowledge of my experience and philosophies, as we both know this is a big hire! Though it may seem like my experience in product is limited, it’s actually very extensive in ways that may not be immediately recognizable. I wanted to show those here and explain them so you can peruse them over the weekend.
I wanted to highlight transferable PM experiences and also marketing experiences, as that’s what you wanted me to explain further. I hope this document gives you a really solid idea of both of those things. 
My Career in Product: 
Sandbox: 
Now comes the Sandbox experience! My first true product team experience in tech, where we had to build something from scratch with very few resources. As you know how Sandbox goes, I wasn’t just the product manager. I was also the salesperson, the researcher, the team motivator, the one learning to code at 2 AM, and the person figuring out how to keep the whole thing from falling apart, as many in cohort 01 came in with many different expectations. Most PMs wanted to build a company, some engineers did, and hardly any UX designers wanted to stay past the one-year commitment. It was wild.
We started as a team of four with four interns. I didn’t pick my co-founders, and I quickly learned how important it is to work with people you jive with, not just smart ones, but the ones who are accountable, adaptable, and clear. It started off good, but as shit hit the fan (as it always does in startups), I realized our team wasn’t aligned, and that had serious consequences for execution. I tried to be transparent with my teammates, as that’s important to me. After one pitch competition, where we were trying to raise money, we found out we didn’t secure funding because most of the VCs didn’t believe our team was the right team to build the product. After individually calling all these VCs to hear their feedback, I shared that with the team, hoping it would be motivating. But I wasn’t as careful with my wording as I should’ve been, and the conversation ended with two people completely checking out and not contributing for the last three months (but I was also stuck with them because this was part of their college credit). It was one of the toughest leadership lessons I’ve ever had when managing a product team. I learned that hard conversations need to be handled clearly, gently, and collaboratively, or they can break the team.
Despite the chaos, we still built something real. I created the bi-monthly sprints. I managed our interns. I built our product without code because our one engineer wasn’t able to produce working code due to the limited abilities the CS program taught at BYU. At that point, we had paying customers. I had been walking business to business, selling this idea. So I figured out how to white-label a solution, customize it, and deliver something usable. It wasn’t perfect, but it proved I could make things happen under pressure. By Demo Day, we were one of only four teams with revenue.
Because of this experience, where, without dedicated and talented engineers, I had to white-label something, I learned how much an engineer really does bring to the team. As much as I wanted to be in every detail, I realized that if I ever wanted to scale a product, I couldn’t micromanage the code. I had to trust, but also verify, and that balance is something I’ve taken seriously ever since. You can have the best idea in the world, but if you can’t ship it, it doesn’t matter. 
You know the startup schedule very well, and in my own way, I do too. I was still in college, working two jobs, performing with BYU’s Young Ambassadors, serving as Elders Quorum President, and coming out as gay for the first time. Somehow, I still spent over 40 hours on Sandbox. Over 8 months, I pulled more than 25 full all-nighters (not just late nights, but actual 48-hour marathons trying to keep things running). I would prefer not to be that unhealthy again, tbh, but when push comes to shove, you gotta do what you gotta do, and I really tried my best to prove that. I dove deep into learning how to be the best PM I could, and I started interviewing product managers, reading books, and taking online coding courses just to keep up and support my team the right way.
We validated our market. We had sales. But in the end, without a reliable technical build, we couldn’t keep going. Eventually, I made the decision to step away and take an internship at Divvy, where I could learn more about product at a company I respected.
I’m ready for the hard work, late nights, and wild experiences that will come with being your first PM. I’ve lived through the kind of chaos most early-stage PMs will only read about, and I am ready to do it again because I’ve come out the other side still obsessed with building products.

Divvy:
My story at Divvy will prove how relentless I can be if I want something (like being hired by you haha! Exhibit A: this fucking long paper with every example possible to try and get you to pick me over all the other people).
So, when I got to Divvy, it wasn’t through a job posting. I really wanted to work at a great company and learn from a product leader (Gentry) I respected and got to know in Sandbox. So I kept emailing and following up with him and Tyler to create an internship for me over the summer. It took me 4 months, but eventually, they created a role just for me where I got to do analytics for all the product teams.
Once I got in, I was handed a project that no one else really wanted to deal with: fix Pendo. Pendo is a tool that tracks what users are doing inside your app (maybe you used it?? I doubt it, as it wasn’t a sales tool, but maybe you did!) It’s supposed to help product teams make better decisions with real data. But at Divvy, most of the product teams weren’t using it (OR ANY DATA!!!!! WHICH IS CRAZYYY) at all. They were just building things based on gut feelings or a few user interviews. Not because they didn’t care—just because the data was messy, hard to read, and disorganized.
So I spent my time interviewing every product pod. I asked them what they liked about Pendo, why they weren’t using it, and what would help. I found a few “Pendo missionaries” who used it well and got value from it, but most of the teams were overwhelmed or confused. There were broken tags, duplicate events, and unclear names. All of it was basically a mess.
I stayed late most nights (sometimes until 1 or 2 in the morning), going through each tag, checking the CSS/HTML behind every button, and making sure the data was accurate. I worked across iOS, mobile, and desktop. I built a clean taxonomy so everything was organized and made sense. Then I created training docs and videos and started walking teams through how to use it. I even presented to all the product teams before I left.
By the end of my 4 months, Pendo had gone from something most people ignored to something they could actually trust and use. One of the product managers even texted Gentry after my presentation and said, “You should hire this guy.” I would have loved to stay, but I had already accepted an internship with Senator Mitt Romney, as coming on full-time wasn’t an option when I started.
The biggest thing I learned from this is that PMs can’t build good products without good data. That sounds obvious, but it’s surprising how many teams still make decisions based on assumptions or a few strong opinions. That’s risky. Product decisions cost time and money, and without clear data, it’s easy to spend both on the wrong thing.
Data will matter so much to me in any role. I will be in it every day. You’re building an AI tool for salespeople who are busy, results-driven, and don’t have time for tons of trial and error. The product needs to feel smooth and useful right away. I want to see what they are doing, what they are not doing, and figure out why. That means knowing the user data, learning where they get stuck, and improving fast. It means building a system that tracks the right stuff from day one so none of us waste time guessing.
If I join your company, I’d bring that same type of data mindset. I truly don’t just want to ship features, I want to make sure we’re solving the right problems. I’ll track what users are doing, find the drop-offs, listen to the data, and help you shape the product based on what’s actually happening, not just what we think is happening.

Crew:
Working at Crew helped me really see all the things I learned in classes or in books in action, for better or for worse.
I was the first product manager at Crew. I was more like Gentry’s associate PM because his thing at Divvy was product, so he was the product guy at Crew. I’d research, design, test, and bring forward my recommendations. He’d make the final calls. But most of the time, I was on my own to figure out what was most important for Crew to do next.
I ran product design, branding, onboarding, user research, card program logistics/supply chain strategy, and marketing. After interviewing multiple people and looking across the country for someone to do our in-app designs, I could not find someone that fit the tight parameters we were wanting at a price we could afford. One day I drew up a mock design to try and show what I wanted the brand to be, and our team decided I should just become our illustrator. So, I internalized the illustration work, and it saved us over $110,000. I used Figma, InDesign, and Procreate (for still and animated designs) to build a flexible brand system that worked across different screen sizes or in different states. Seeing my art on cards, in the app, or on billboards was great after all this work of trying to find the right brand. Testing it was interesting as well. Whenever we had someone come in for onboarding testing, without fail or being prompted, they mentioned how much they liked the brand and illustrations. It didn’t feel like a typical bank to them, and that was something they really liked. It was great to hear unprompted positive feedback on something I worked really hard on to make as right as possible.
The challenge was that our product was for families, and families are complicated. For example, should I show a traditional nuclear family? What about single parents, LGBTQ+ families, or kids with disabilities? What if showing a dad reminds someone of their dad who died? What if someone doesn’t have a traditional family? I decided the brand shouldn’t depict families at all. Instead, I built a visual system based on symbols that could convey what I was trying to present: money, connection, kids, adulthood, and nostalgia. It gave us a way to represent belonging without pushing specific images that could alienate people. That may not sound like a big decision, but it helped shape how people felt when they interacted with our product. The microexperiences add up over time.
I also led our onboarding experience. Morgan, our designer, and I had great collaborative experiences. He was the exact opposite of me, and we had the same desire to create something great, which honestly unified us. We would go back and forth to find the right balance between usability and brand, function and emotion. We tested our flows live with users often, listened to what they said, and paid attention to what they didn’t say. I’m a huge believer in the Kano Model, which focuses on making sure the basics are met, performance is high, and there are delighters throughout. All of these are needed for a standout product. Most only focus on the first two, and if they can, they’ll add delighters. Delighters are harder to validate, though, and often aren’t as easy to quantify. Delighters come from unprompted verbal exclamations or through eyebrow raises, little smiles, or quiet “oh” moments. That’s what I looked for in our testing. It’s moving past asking what users want and providing them with a tool that can make them feel positive.
I also tried to push us harder on messaging. We didn’t have a budget for Facebook ad tests, so I took our homepage on an iPad and went to Traverse Mountain to ask parents what they thought we were selling. I recorded their reactions, played them for the team, and redesigned the page four more times based on what I heard. By version five, people finally understood what the product was and how it helped them. But in the end, Gentry went back to the original version he created, which was the one we’d started with. That was hard to see, as I admired Gentry. Still do. But I learned a very valuable lesson from that. I learned that even when the data says to do one thing, not everyone wants to do that. It is really hard to let go of our own ideas and believe the insights in the data. I love the use of psychology in product design. It takes it over the top—from a tool to something that you connect with (sounds cheesy, but ChatGPT, Trader Joe’s, Tesla, or even musicians do it all the time). Creating a Story Brand is a framework I believe every company should champion and one I tried to implement at Crew, though psychology principles weren’t seen as a better way to go than intuition.
I have to admit, I do not know a lot of things. I really don’t. And because of that, I will always default to trusting someone accredited first rather than someone who isn’t. I want to test accredited ideas before I have to reinvent the wheel. We need to move too fast in a startup to always be recreating the wheel. That is why process is so crucial. If that process is not working, then you can take the time to reinvent the wheel if needed, and hopefully fewer wheels will need to be reinvented, saving time, money, and ultimately being more effective. I am an advocate of building brand’s around the Story Brand framework. It’s a sales framework translated to a marketing use case, and it knows how to sell a product.
And that was the core tension for me at Crew. I cared deeply about what we were building. My role as a PM is to help us reach product-market fit, and I will do everything I can to do that, but if I am unable to do that, then my role becomes obsolete. But when I raised issues like us skipping core product principles or building features that didn’t solve real problems, I was often ignored, and my inexperience was often touted as the reason. But because of my newness to the fintech field, I really wanted to make sure I knew what I was doing, so I dove deep into trying to understand the user. This helped me do my job by seeing things others didn’t, because I was closest to the customer. That’s what made it frustrating. To be clear, I believe in a founder’s right to choose the direction. It’s their company. Their vision. But I also believe they deserve team members who will be honest, who will do the research, and bring real options to the table. That’s what I tried to do. And even when decisions went against what data said, I’m proud I did the work to lead my team in the best direction possible.
Leaving Crew was very difficult, and I didn’t want to leave, but I couldn’t be a PM there. It went against so many of the best practices and principles that make a truly great product. I want to be a PM in a place that loves data, thinks of the user first, and finds what we can build that will grow the business, and deeply cares about having strong discussions and not a yes-man culture.
I want to be part of a team that seems like the team that actually wants to lean into product principles from the start. You’re trying to build fast but also make sure everything feels intuitive. The product can’t just work. It has to feel like it gets them. It truly has to be at least 10x better. If not, no one will convert. That is incredibly hard to do. A lot of people think it needs to just be a little better, but it needs to be way better in all the right ways. Doing product correctly is incredibly hard, and doing it right won’t happen without real user research, clean feedback loops, fast iteration, refined marketing, and a tool that, once someone has used it, they cannot believe they lived without before.
I will bring that hard work that is needed to ship solutions that are worth building, and the willingness to challenge what isn’t for us.

Utah Business: 
Every product role I’ve had has involved selling, not just building. That’s not common for most PMs, but I think it should be. Selling forces you to understand your product in a different way. You see the gaps more clearly, and you realize fast whether something actually resonates or not.
Utah Business is my first full-time sales role. I was recruited as an Account Executive, so I’m not on the product side anymore. It has been a huge asset for me because I now understand what it really feels like to be on the front lines at a large company that is a sales-first company over a product and customer company. I know what sales teams are asked to do now, how quotas work, what CRMs look like day to day, how outreach gets tracked, and what kind of pressure reps are under. That experience gives me way more context walking into a company. I’m not pretending to know everything about everyone’s sales style, but I at least know better how to interview salespeople, which will make me a much better PM when doing user research.
At Utah Business, I consult with companies not just about magazine placements, but also print ads, email campaigns, digital marketing, SEO, custom publications, billboards, TV, radio, and more. We have a full agency team that supports the execution, but I’m the one helping clients figure out what actually makes sense for them or what fits what they want to try. That gives me a front-row seat to what people are spending money on, the prices for these marketing placements, what works best depending on company size and goals, and what they expect to get out of it.
This work has made me much sharper at marketing strategy. It’s also made me quicker to spot BS. I understand now that marketing is going to be rough if the product sucks. If it’s not selling, the product needs to be looked at first. That is why it is good to have PMMs or those in product helping to craft the marketing, because they can see what people are thinking it should do based on the marketing and what it actually does. You can iterate on messaging and make sure bottlenecks are diminished as much as humanly possible to make the most efficient marketing messaging possible.
A core belief of mine is that sales and product should not be disconnected. That may not be a common take in the product world, but it is a philosophy I have seen benefit sales teams time and time again, and I see great product fail when those are separated. Sales knows the customer well. They hear every objection, every hesitation, every point of confusion. But they often don’t know why certain features can’t be prioritized. On the flip side, product teams might have a tech limitation so they can’t implement a feature so easily, but they miss the nuance in how people are actually reacting to the product. Both sides need to talk more. I bring that understanding with me. I know how to be a translator between those teams.
I’ve also used internal tools like Monday.com to manage campaigns, build workflows, and keep myself organized across more than 25 products we sell each month. We all have areas we specialize in, but we also support clients across the board. So I’ve had to stay sharp on everything from our annual awards to local SEO packages. That variety has trained my process mindset as well as my marketing know-how.
This builds on what I did at Divvy, where I worked with PMMs to write in-product Pendo guides so users actually understood how to use the product. That’s internal and external communication experience I can carry straight into a product marketing or onboarding initiative.
Between Divvy, Crew, and Utah Business, I’ve gotten a well-rounded view of product, marketing, and sales. I know how to test messaging. I know what it feels like to sell something users want or don’t. And I know how to work with cross-functional teams, figure out how people are using a tool, and build something that actually helps.
Additional Product Experience: 
Archway Construction:

I want to start off my additional work experience section with this project as it is a rare experience that highlights my leadership, vision, ambition, ability to figure things out, and manage a team that is tasked with a very logistically difficult project. When I talk about other experiences in tech or otherwise, I often am working in a team (which is how it should be done), and it is hard to know if the outcome is because of Brant, the team, or someone else. This experience is solely mine, where I had to lead a team. It was truly a team effort as I could not have done it without dozens of people making it possible, but there was no one to pick up my slack if I had some. If I weren’t leading the project, it would not have gotten done, nor would it have even existed in the first place, so this will show what I am capable of to the highest level, and you then will be able to use this as a benchmark for everything else I discuss in this document.

When I was 18, I decided to rebuild an archway that used to stand at the entrance of my high school for 50 years. The old one would not work any longer and was dated. It needed modernizing. The original had been torn down during renovations, and the school had no plans to replace it. So I sketched up a new design that was much grander than the previous and presented it to the administration. The principal told me, “If you can get the money for it, you can build it.” That was my green light.


(Old, smaller archway to the left, which was erected in the 1950s and taken down in 2012. It then sat broken apart, rusting behind the school, so putting it back up was not an option as it would not fit the newly expanded road and needed a facelift anyway.) 

The archway project wasn’t easy. Sponsors were hesitant. One even said, “Things like this never actually get completed.” I had no background in welding, electrical, blueprints, or really anything that could make this project happen, but I was determined to get it done. I managed a team of people with way more technical knowledge than me, coordinated with local businesses, and raised over $100,000 in total value: $70,000 in donated labor and services, and $30,000 in cash for materials and concrete.
The project also taught me early product management lessons. User testing was a big one. My first design placed a “U” (our school’s logo) in the middle of the word “Uintah,” and four people thought it said “Uin Utah.” That was my first lesson in how easy it is to miss your own blind spots and how important it is to listen to users. Only four out of 500+ people who saw the design (which had gone viral on social media) brought it up, but it highlighted something important: the 500 people knew the brand well and could guess what I meant, but the four, who also knew the brand, were brave enough to say what someone unfamiliar with the brand would think.

I brushed it off a few times, thinking “everyone’s a critic” and that it wasn’t a big deal. But when I heard it for the fourth and final time, it hit me: this is how people are going to view the archway for the next 50 years. So I changed it. I went back to the blueprint designers and requested a redesign. It was a small ask compared to the time and donations (up to $100,000) that would be wasted if people were confused. Pivot when things are cheap and easy, not when it’s late. That’s why feedback is crucial and why PMs shouldn’t be too beholden to their own ideas. I’ll defend my ideas, but when I know I’m wrong, I’ll concede. I’m not a yes-man or a pushover, but I try hard to admit fault the moment I recognize it. Staying on a sinking ship doesn’t help anyone, right?
Another PM lesson is watching for feature creep syndrome. I overbuilt the archway, which is a common pitfall in product management. I added outlets for events, hooks for banners, and fake security cameras. Still to this day, no matter how many people I’ve told about these features, none have been used. No one has hung a banner. No one’s used the outlets. It taught me a critical lesson: just because you think something is valuable doesn’t mean others do. It might be too much work for them, or it simply might not be a real need. Even after training people, they still might not want what you built.
That’s the 80/20 rule in action. I spent so much time thinking through how the banners would be hung and how the outlets could be used, and it didn’t matter because I was the only one who cared or saw the benefit. Do I still believe they are good features? Damn sure. But those who actually can use those features don’t, even though I would if I was back in school.
Some features I added weren’t meant to be used but were implemented as strategic bets for future growth, which is important for PMs to think through. You have to weigh immediate needs and future tradeoffs. It’s a hard decision (no one can predict the future, though data can help). I didn’t really have a data tool for this project, though. But the future is coming no matter what.
That’s why I designed the archway in modular parts. It can be disassembled, moved, or updated if the school ever needs to. I raised the arch an extra five feet so the curve wouldn’t block bus clearance if they ever expanded the road. These were the reasons it was taken down in the first place, so I planned for that to happen again. I also made sure the school name could be changed without tearing the whole structure down, as that has been floated many times. I tried to think through every future scenario that could affect the core product (the archway) and make sure the investment was worth it.
The project stalled while I was away on my mission. I tried to hand it off to five different adults, but no one could get it done. That was incredibly stressful. As I mentioned, some donors told me it would never happen. I wanted to prove them wrong, but I had no control at that point, and it was a very complex project with a lot of moving parts. Once I came home, I picked it back up and finally got it finished.
I had so many problems to solve that they don’t teach you in school (or college, for that matter haha). I dealt with legal permitting issues that could have raised costs. The school district required me to install a new electrical meter with the county (something that was completely unnecessary but required by their bureaucracy), which highlights a product principle: sometimes in product, you have regulations you have to follow. It may not be obvious to the user, but security, privacy, or tech stack decisions can make or break a product. Even though they don’t feel like a huge need to worry about now, if you ignore them, lawsuits will kill you fast. PMs need to mitigate these costs and keep product teams happy and users coming back.
I also handled all the fundraising without help from the school and had to navigate a new superintendent who almost shut the archway down over a clerical error from a former finance secretary. I was able to lean on my relationships with the school board, and they stepped in so the project could move forward. People will be against innovation, but we need to fight and not back down. That is also a job of a PM: to make sure the needs they are trying to find a solution for are solved.
After it was completed, the school board honored me for designing, managing, and engaging the community in something so ambitious, and that really showed me that no matter how young someone is or how little they know, they can do incredible things if they have a vision and can bring the right team together.
The archway is now a community landmark in my town. Seniors take graduation photos under it every year, and it’s always featured in the school’s marketing materials. But more than that, it stands for something to me: vision, commitment, and the ability to finish something hard. I want to build something that impacts billions of people. I want to go far beyond this—not out of pride, but because I genuinely believe I’m wired to enjoy and thrive in environments like this.

I want to see the team go on to build even more things that heal the world. I want you to start your fund! Like, that makes me so hyped! I want to give my best to something that matters and multiply its impact through hard, thoughtful work.

Scholarship:
Under that archway, I started something else: the Uintah Resilience Scholarship. While I was student body president, I met weekly with school counselors to talk about student mental health, which is something I started to do because of my own encounters with it. I kept seeing students who were working multiple jobs, raising siblings, or battling incredibly tough circumstances for a teenager, and those students were rarely the ones getting scholarships or being recognized. That didn’t sit right with me.
So I took leftover funds from the archway and started a $1,000 annual scholarship for a student who’s shown real resilience. Not perfect grades. Not packed extracurriculars. Just grit. I’ve now given out six scholarships, and I plan to keep going. No one in their 20s or 30s had ever started a scholarship fund at my high school before. And I don’t have millions of dollars. But I saw a need, and I did something about it.

This story might not be about a tech product, but it is about product thinking to me. It’s about having a purpose behind building and shipping something meaningful. I coordinated dozens of people, handled real fundraising, and balanced tradeoffs to create this scholarship. It is small (though the second-largest scholarship possible to receive at my high school), but if I am going to go through all the work of building something like a massive archway, I want to find meaning in it. It’s just how I am.
I may not have 10 years of product experience, but I care about the people I am building for and I know you do too.

My product experience and my unique experience on a Mormon Mission:
	Like, I know this experience isn’t wildly unique, but there is an aspect of mine that really was, so I want to share it.
My new mission president called me and asked if I could fix the way we were doing all our reporting. It was this giant spreadsheet that was not user-friendly at all and was taking him hours just to get through each week. He knew I was creative, enjoyed building things, and was a really dedicated worker, so even though I didn’t know how to code, he wanted me to figure out how to make this actually work for him.
They assigned me a service missionary as my companion, which meant I was doing all the work solo, and that was my only focus for six weeks as we could not proselyte. The product skills started early—I had to learn what the mission president needed, what the assistants to the president needed, and how the missionaries were actually filling out this info. Most of them were doing it on their phones, a few on tablets. I was building on a computer, so I had to keep checking if it translated to mobile. Also, we were only allowed to use Google Suite apps, so nothing outside of that. I had to work within those limits, which is a daily tradeoff for PMs.
I spent hours every day on YouTube learning formulas for Google Sheets and basic Google Script to get it to function like a tool instead of just a time-sucking, horribly messy, and not-at-all-helpful spreadsheet. The trickiest part was making sure each person only saw what they needed (i.e., district leaders were limited to their districts, zone leaders couldn’t see other zones, assistants needed everything, and the president needed it all in a summary that actually made sense). I also had to make sure it followed the UK’s strict privacy laws, which I didn’t know much about at the time, but with tightening rules, I knew was very important to the Church.
By the end of six weeks, I built something that took our assistants’ calls from 8 hours a week down to 15 minutes. It was clean, accurate, way easier to use, and not breakable by missionaries.
My marketing comes into play where, after that, I helped rebrand the mission to match the Church’s look. My president cared a lot about design and the experience people had at conferences, so I started doing all the branding for events: slides, invites, handouts, agendas, videos, and new handout cards. Anything people saw, I designed it. I also planned and marketed conferences so they felt intentional and on-brand for my mission president.
Eventually, Church headquarters found out what we were doing and reached out. I worked with them to give feedback on their Missionary Planner app so leadership across the world could track what we were tracking. We helped shape what data was being collected and how to make it easier for everyone. Our mission even got access to Instagram before most others because of how we were pushing tech in thoughtful ways. I didn’t get to use it before I went home, but I submitted the request, so that was cool.
Looking back, I didn’t realize it at the time, but I was doing product research, engineering, UX, analytics, and even legal (because of the UK privacy rules). And I was building a tool for different user types, with different needs, all inside one system. It worked, and it made people’s lives easier.
It also taught me how fast people can break something if it’s not designed well and how important it is to simplify things. Even stuff I thought was cool ended up confusing people. So I had to learn not to build for myself, but for the people actually using it and test it. Something I was able to build upon from the learnings from the archway project.

MPA:
I didn’t plan to work for the BYU Master of Public Administration department. I just had a deep interest in local government and started reaching out to cities and counties on my own time. That curiosity led the MPA program to invite me to join their research team. It was a unique experience, as I was the only undergrad and only non-MPA student allowed on the project.
The goal was to create a multi-year research project analyzing local government structures and employment needs so universities could prepare their students effectively. I came in at the very beginning, helping set up the structure and develop the key research questions we’d later run through R. I didn’t realize it at the time, but this was my first exposure to something very close to product interviews: talking to real people to figure out what matters, what they’re frustrated with, and what employment needs they had and not just what we thought theirs were.
We pulled insights from over 250 interviews with local government leaders and departments. I helped refine the research, cleaned and analyzed the data using R, and modeled sentimental trends in what they were saying. The goal was to translate hundreds of qualitative responses into something we could actually act on. That process, where we distilled complex, often messy inputs (interviews) into something structured, proved how you can gain product insights from qualitative data as an additional tool to your quantitative data.
While I was there, the department head also asked me to redo their entire WordPress website. I had never touched WordPress before, but I figured it out. I rebuilt the site structure, updated SEO and domain setup, redesigned contact forms, and improved user flow. I didn’t know it then, but this was my crash course in digital marketing, backend logic, and how design impacts trust and clarity. It’s also where I first started thinking about landing pages not as decoration, but as a product in themselves that had objectives and friction points. Though not seen as a PM role, I was doing PM work that taught me further how to conduct user tests, especially when it comes to setting up systems for when results need further analysis.

Bonus experiences that impact my Product Management philosophies: 
Politics: 
Most people don’t associate government work with product management, but it shaped the way I think about users.
I’ve had the chance to work for several government entities: local, state, and federal. I started out as the first-ever executive intern for the Vernal City Manager when I was 16, where I worked directly with city departments on community development projects, such as helping manage $250K in public health grants. These types of projects teach you how to break down complex problems, align people across departments, and push projects forward. What I learned here is a key product philosophy. You can have a transformational idea, but if people don’t know about it, know how to use it, and make it insanely easy to access, no one will use it. Our incentives to use $250K to make people healthier were not the incentives of the citizens. To change behavior, you either have to follow those 3 steps or make sure your incentives are aligned with your audience. This is something product managers have to think through each time they implement a solution.
I did marketing for the county next. One of the most defining parts of this work was putting on 20+ events and conferences, including the Utah Economic & Energy Summit and the Utah Tourism Conference. I helped organize the 2017 Utah Symphony performance at Dinosaur National Monument, coordinating everything from sponsors to logistics, and also helped lead the marketing effort for the Uintah County Travel Board that year. Marketing events is not an easy task. The right desires need to be in place for people to attend. We worked with hundreds of community partners to make sure our events were successful, and that was a key learning experience.
From there, I worked at the Utah Governor’s Office managing constituent needs. A key learning was that everyone has an opinion and to not throw out everything just because one person said something. In product, you have to say no a lot. It is a key part of the job. You cannot build everything, and that is okay. You need to do what is most advantageous for the company and the customers, and it is your job to figure out what that is amongst a lot of other ideas or opinions.
At the Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity, I was once again in marketing. Here, I helped manage the award-winning statewide “In Utah” COVID campaign, built messaging for CARES Act grant programs, and coordinated communication across 13 channels. I advised nearly 1,000 businesses on how to apply for aid and helped them navigate the federal system. That taught me a lot about crisis communication, and about what happens when clarity, timing, and execution really matter. It also taught me that marketing doesn’t exist in a silo. The head of marketing needs external firms to do a lot of things as they do not have control of some channels of distribution. A marketer’s job is to know when to do it in-house (or even if you can) and when or who to bring in to help execute on the matters you don’t have access to.
Working for Senator Romney taught me about leadership. He was incredibly attentive and knew how to diffuse situations like no one I had ever seen. Though he was the most experienced in the entire room, he would patiently wait to hear from every person on his team. Leading product means you need to know a lot of things, but you entrust others on your team to know more than you do and to allow them to be the experts. I am not an engineer or a designer, and my job is to let them thrive in their expertise while also making sure they are aligned with the realities of the situation. I was also tasked with understanding nuclear policy (like isn’t that crazy? Haha). Senator Romney’s staffers needed to know how to advise him on some nuclear grants. I had to figure out the timeline and phases of what companies had to go through for some SMRs and if the government should continue to fund it. What was hard about this is that I was asked to find information that didn’t exist. No one had ever completed this process, and that wasn’t known at the beginning. So I had to call many people to figure out what the process was, where companies were along in that process, and how much longer it would cost to complete. The issue is there are countless ways to get approved, so there was not a clear path to approval. It was a complex process, one no one knew much about, and I had to figure it all out to be able to inform the senator. There are a lot of similarities with creating product, as we are going into uncharted territory with AI and our new product. I am someone who can handle ambiguity and uncertainty, even with some of the most complex topics.
Why politics is relevant to product rolese is that it has multiple stakeholders, strict budgets, dozens of moving pieces, and a need to get things right the first time under the scrutiny of citizens who are very difficult to please and inform. Politics, at its core, is about people. Your job is to serve your constituents, understand their concerns, earn their trust, and communicate solutions in a way that resonates. Being a PM has lots of parallels. You’re building for people, and if you don’t spend time learning how they think, what they care about, and what they’re actually trying to solve for, you’re just guessing and that is not true product.
This kind of experience matters when I’m building a product for salespeople, and sales is all about persuasion, timing, and empathy which is very similar to politics. You’re also operating in a space where brand, clarity, and user value are everything, and I’ve learned how to make things happen when there’s no playbook.

Theatre: 
Most people see the parallels between sports and business, but I think there are more connections between theatre and business. At the end of the day, everything people in business are creating is for an audience or users. At its core, theatre is about creating something that makes people feel something. You rehearse, refine, and build an experience so the audience walks away changed, or at the very least, connected to the message you were trying to convey. That’s not so different from product work, as the user experience will make or break the product.
When someone uses a product, they’re stepping into a “show.” If we don’t get the flow right (scene transitions), the screens or tools (set pieces), the messaging (script), the product mix (the storyline), the UX experience (costumes/consistency), or the technical performance (lighting or microphones), the users will leave feeling confused or like they wasted their time. In theatre, when the performance feels forced or disconnected, the audience checks out. Same with product. And if no one knows what your show’s about in the first place? They don’t show up. That’s where marketing and clarity come in.
When I was in high school, I led a full marketing campaign for our theatre department. I built our first social media ad strategy, transformed the school itself into an immersive version of the show using just a $500 budget, and pulled together a 10-person student team to help. We sold out 1,200 seats every night of a 12-day run my junior and senior year when I began doing this. This was something that’s never happened before or since. That experience taught me that if you want people to show up, you have to make the experience known and worth it. Then create a stellar show (product). Those years we were top 10 in the state and even won best in the state one of those years.
This unique experience applies directly to building and launching products: if users don’t understand the value and it fails to deliver on that value, it’ll be an expensive flop.
Another example is when I performed with Elf: The Musical at Hale Centre Theatre, where you can see every face in the crowd. Here you can see subtle reactions in real time from the audience such as boredom, confusion, or delight. This is live A/B testing. You don’t need a data chart to tell you if lines or jokes are landing with the audience because you can see it. That skill helps me during user testing and live feedback sessions: knowing what people say is one thing, but how they react, or don’t, tells you more.
I’ve also been in shows where the “product” failed because we didn’t test it. At BYU, I was part of the Young Ambassadors tour where the director (who had been on Broadway) decided to write a brand-new show. It told three unrelated stories with music and choreography that didn’t fit the lyrics. The director did not test this show, like is customary to do when creating a new show, and because we didn’t test it in front of an audience first, it flopped and was canceled after one year. The next year, we switched to a well-tested show, and it was such a success we toured it in South Korea. It reminded me that even the most experienced leaders, even ones on Broadway, can get it wrong if they don’t listen to the audience or validate the direction.
That principle is just as true in product. You can have the best team, the best funding, the smartest people, but if you skip testing or assume you know better than your users or audience, you’ll fail. Broadway’s “New York, New York” was created by all the greats and still closed early because it didn’t connect. Even top-tier creators can miss if they ignore feedback. I’ve seen feedback ignored in every aspect of my life and it always is a bad decision. I am feedback-focused. It’s how I can have any type of confidence that of the million different ideas or things we could build, this one is good because we are getting the reactions and responses we want from the users.
I also believe that being a PM isn’t about being the star of the show. I see the PM role as supporting the Director: the CEO. As a product person, I see myself as an Assistant Director. I’m not in charge of costumes, lighting, or set designs, but I am responsible for making sure all those moving parts support the CEO’s vision and that the audience (our users) resonate with what we have built.
Theatre also taught me the value of mess. Rehearsals are messy. Choreography has missteps. Props break. People miss cues. But it’s that process that gets refined over time, that makes something great and real. I love that part. I love shaping something rough into something remarkable. The same way we fix transitions, tighten lines, and polish timing on stage, we iterate on user flows, refine messaging, and craft features because they make sense. That’s how good products get built.
So whether it’s launching a new feature, building a better onboarding experience, or refining our go-to-market messaging, I bring this mindset to product. People don’t come to a product just for functionality, they come hoping it will do something for them. That’s the show. And if we can make it feel intuitive, enjoyable, and memorable, they’ll keep coming back and tell their friends. Just like any great performance.
